summary:
AstroSanté is a medical monitoring station for the flight surgeon of a space mission. It runs offline, with no AI and no network. It continuously receives data from personally assigned wearable sensors (oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose and radiation), 24 hours a day, sleep included.

The program analyzes this data over a sliding 2-minute window, detects 22 syndromes and proposes a short, structured course of action: actions, treatment with dosages, escalation and monitoring. It also tracks cumulative radiation dose against reference limits.

This project addresses a real problem: on an isolated mission, the physician must quickly detect physiological drift and radiation exposure without a reliable connection. Every measurement and every decision is recorded locally. The program proposes, the physician decides. Built in PowerShell, it runs as a single file with no installation.
details:
"Describe your project in detail. Answer the following questions: What does it do, or how does it work? What benefits does it bring? What impact do you expect? What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did you use to develop it? What makes your project creative? What factors did your team consider?"

Here is a draft answer in English, based on the files you shared. Check the points marked in brackets, since I only know what is in your documents.

What it does and how it works

AstroSanté is a medical monitoring station for the flight surgeon of a space mission. It runs offline, with no AI and no network. It continuously receives data from personally assigned wearable sensors, 24 hours a day including sleep, and tracks seven indicators: oxygen saturation, heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, temperature, blood glucose and radiation dose rate. Each indicator is shown with a status (normal, caution, alert or critical). Sensors are read every 30 seconds. A sensor is flagged offline after 5 minutes, and a signal loss after a critical value is flagged at 30 minutes.

Every 2 minutes of data are analyzed over a sliding window. The software detects 22 syndromes and produces a short, structured course of action: level and summary, actions, radiological analysis, treatment (dose, route, maximum, contraindications), escalation and monitoring. It includes 14 built-in drug sheets. The interface is a single window with four tabs: Detail, Physician Data, Report and Initial Diagnosis. Without real sensors, it starts in simulation mode with 6 astronaut profiles.

Benefits

  • The flight surgeon gets a quick, consistent first assessment instead of reading raw values.
  • It works in isolated environments, because it needs no network, no cloud and no external dependency.
  • Every measurement, alert and course of action is recorded locally, which gives full traceability.
  • The program proposes and the physician decides, so clinical responsibility stays with the doctor.
  • Radiation is handled in two ways: instantaneous dose rate, and cumulative dose compared with 30-day and annual limits. This matters in space, where exposure builds up over time.

Expected impact

  • Earlier detection of physiological drift and of radiation exposure.
  • A faster, more standardized response, with a clear escalation path.
  • A lighter workload for the medical team during long missions.
  • Better medical records, through automatic logging and a "Copy the course of action" function.
  • The same approach could extend to other isolated or remote settings, such as polar stations, offshore platforms or field hospitals.

Tools and technologies used

  • Language: PowerShell, with a graphical interface built on Windows Forms (.NET).
  • Launcher: a Windows batch file (.bat).
  • Data formats: JSON for configuration, astronaut profiles and sensor input, and CSV for measurement, alert and course-of-action logs.
  • Design: a single script with no external libraries, no database and no installation.
  • Hardware: wearable sensors writing JSON files, replaced by a realistic simulation of 6 astronaut profiles for testing. [Add the actual sensor hardware if you used any.]

What makes it creative

  • It delivers a clinical decision-support engine without any AI, using transparent, rule-based logic the physician can understand and verify.
  • The whole system is one script that runs from a double-click.
  • It adds a radiation dosimetry layer, integrating dose rate over time, to what is otherwise a vital-signs monitor.
  • The simulation includes realistic personal profiles and rare radiation excursions, so the software can be demonstrated and tested without hardware.
  • The output format is always the same, which makes it quick to read in an emergency.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety and responsibility: the tool is decision support only. Thresholds and dosages must be validated by space medicine before any real use.
  • Reliability in isolation: offline operation, and clear flags for sensor loss.
  • Traceability: local logging of all data and decisions.
  • Simplicity: minimal interface and no dependencies.
  • Privacy and access: the Physician Data tab is reserved for the flight surgeon.
  • Known limits: only the last 6,000 measurements per astronaute are kept in memory, so the cumulative dose is underestimated beyond that. Authentication, network synchronization and PDF export are out of scope for this version.

If the form has a character limit, tell me the limit and I'll shorten it. I can also add your team's own factors, such as roles, constraints or testing.
